Before
 Hon'Ble Shri Justice B. P. Sharma
 On The 31st Of March, 2026
 Misc. Criminal Case No. 44251 of 2024
BHAVYA JAIN AND OTHERS  Versus
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH AND OTHERS  Appearance:
Shri Siddhant Kochar appeared for petitioners.

Shri Piyush Gupta, Advocate for the respondent No.2.
 Shri Manish Mukhariya - PL for State.
 ORDER

This petition has been filed invoking the inherent powers of this Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. for quashing the FIR dated 03.09.2022 bearing Crime No. 171/2022 registered at Police Station Salamatpur, District Raisen, for offences under Sections 420 and 34 of the IPC, as well as all consequential proceedings, including the charge sheet dated 15.12.2022.
2.
As per the prosecution, Crime No. 171/2022 was registered at Police Station Salamatpur under Section 420 read with Section 34 of the IPC against the petitioners.
It is alleged that an agreement dated 06.12.2021 was fraudulently executed between the petitioners and the complainant for the sale of a flour plant for a consideration of Rs. 1 crore.
An amount of Rs. 21,00,000/- was paid as earnest money, with the balance payable at the time of execution of the sale deed.

The petitioners allegedly misrepresented the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:25586 2 MCRC-44251-2024 extent of the loan secured on the property, stating it to be Rs. 21,00,000/-,
whereas the actual outstanding amount was about Rs. 1.40 crore.
It is claimed that, had this fact been disclosed, the complainant would not have entered into the agreement.
When the complainant demanded a refund of the earnest money, the petitioners refused, leading to the filing of the complaint and registration of the FIR.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the dispute is purely civil in nature and that the complainant is exerting undue pressure to evade contractual obligations.

It is further submitted that the petitioners' representations led to the registration of a Non-Cognizable Report (NCR)
against the complainant, which, being a public document, reflects the true factual position.
The present FIR is alleged to be a counter-blast to the prior proceedings initiated by the petitioners.

They also entered into another sale agreement to arrange sufficient funds to clear all dues and convey the property free from encumbrances.
The complainant was fully aware of the outstanding loan, as evident from prior discussions and communications, and all material facts were disclosed at the inception.
It is further submitted that, as per the terms of the agreement, any charges on the property were to be borne by the seller.

Learned counsel further contended that respondent No. 2,
by lodging the FIR, has attempted to convert a civil dispute into a criminal one and to exert pressure on the petitioners for the return of the amount allegedly paid.

2026:MPHC-JBP:25586 3 MCRC-44251-2024 argued that criminal courts are not meant to be used for settling civil disputes or pressurizing parties.
It is also contended that respondent No. 2 has simultaneously initiated civil and criminal proceedings for the same cause of action, amounting to an abuse of the process of law.
4. Learned counsel for the State and the complainant opposed the petition and submitted that a prima facie case under Section 420 of the IPC is made out.

The petitioners, by concealing material facts, fraudulently executed the agreement dated 06.12.2021 for the sale of the flour plant for Rs. 1 crore, misrepresenting that the only liability was a loan of Rs. 21,00,000/-, whereas the actual outstanding amount was about Rs. 1.40 crore, thereby attracting criminal liability.
It is further submitted that the pendency of a civil suit does not bar criminal proceedings.
Hence, no interference is warranted and the petition deserves to be dismissed.

5. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material available on record.
6.

Upon hearing learned counsel for the parties and perusal of the entire material available on record, this Court is of the considered opinion that the present case, in substance, arises out of a contractual transaction between the parties and has been given a colour of criminality without the necessary ingredients of the alleged offence being satisfied.

7. From a careful reading of the agreement dated 06.12.2021, which forms the foundation of the dispute, it is manifest that the parties had consciously entered into a sale agreement for sale of a flour plant for a total NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:25586 4 MCRC-44251-2024 consideration of Rs.1 crore.

The agreement itself clearly records that the property in question was financed through Indian Bank, T.T. Nagar Branch, Bhopal, and further stipulates that all charges,
encumbrances and liabilities over the said property were to be cleared by the petitioners/sellers prior to execution of the sale deed.
The agreement to sale demonstrates that the existence of loan liability was not concealed, but rather formed part of the contractual understanding between the parties.

The chronology of events thus indicates that the present FIR is a consequence of a contractual disagreement and appears to be a counterblast to earlier proceedings as the aforesaid property has been sold out by the petitioner to the third person.
8. The essential ingredient to constitute an offence under Section 420 of the IPC is the existence of dishonest or fraudulent intention at the very inception of the transaction.

In the present case, the agreement itself acknowledges the existence of financial encumbrances and places the obligation Bhavya Jain vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 31 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19091440/
2 upon the sellers to clear the same before execution of the sale deed.

sentences.text: When such a stipulation is part of the contract, the allegation that the complainant was deceived on account of the loan liability loses its foundation.
At best, the allegations pertain to non-fulfilment of contractual terms or failure to discharge obligations within the agreed timeframe, which would give rise to civil consequences alone.

9. This Court is of the view that the grievance of the complainant essentially pertains to enforcement of contractual rights, namely, either refund of the earnest money or completion of the transaction.
Such reliefs NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-JBP:25586 5 MCRC-44251-2024 fall squarely within the domain of civil court.

The appropriate remedy available to the complainant, in the facts of the case, is to institute a civil suit for specific performance of contract or for recovery of the alleged amount, as the case may be.
Invocation of criminal machinery for settlement of such disputes amounts to misuse of the process of law.

The continuation of criminal proceedings in the present case, therefore, would amount to permitting coercive processes of the criminal law to be employed for enforcing a purely civil claim, which is impermissible.
The dispute between the parties, being predominantly civil in nature arising out of a contractual relationship, does not disclose commission of any cognizable offence.
10. In view of the foregoing analysis, this Court finds that no prima facie offence under Sections 420 and 34 of the IPC is made out against the petitioners.
Accordingly, the petition is allowed.

The FIR dated 03.09.2022 bearing Crime No. 171/2022 registered at Police Station Salamatpur, District Raisen, as well as the charge-sheet dated 15.12.2022 and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, are hereby quashed.
